content: The method of active case detection (ACD) does not require additional resources or efforts as it is already integrated into the existing healthcare system. However, it has been found to be costly for patients with kala-azar (KA) and post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) who often seek multiple types of healers before receiving a proper diagnosis in public or private healthcare facilities. The choice of ACD approach, including passive case detection (PCD), depends on the situation. The blanket approach is considered the gold standard but is recommended only during outbreak situations due to its high cost. In countries where the healthcare system allows integration of ACD with other health activities, such as family planning, the cost may not be a significant barrier. The camp approach is highly effective for detecting new KA and PKDL cases in areas with high KA endemicity. In contrast, the index case approach is preferred in areas with moderate-to-low KA endemicity or where households are scattered. An incentive-based ACD approach can be particularly useful in low-endemic areas or in combination with other methods. This approach may also employ a snowball technique to identify new KA and PKDL cases but requires careful supervision to prevent misuse of funds. PCD is already in place in all three countries studied and is effective in areas with high community awareness about KA and PKDL, where health services are actively involved in disease control. The frequency of ACD depends on the method used. For the camp approach, conducting it twice a year is sufficient to identify a significant number of new KA and PKDL cases. The index case and incentive-based approaches should be implemented year-round. The blanket approach is reserved for outbreak situations. Cost estimates for different ACD methods vary. PCD, despite its limitations, benefits from being integrated into the public health system. ACD, which is crucial during the disease elimination phase, incurs additional costs ranging from approximately $20 to $600 per new case detected. Among ACD methods, the blanket approach is the most expensive, followed by the incentive-based, camp, and index case approaches. The validation process for eliminating kala-azar as a public health problem in South-East Asia involves specific standard operating procedures (SOPs) for each ACD method. For the index case-based approach, the procedure includes identifying and training health workers, conducting neighborhood searches around index cases, and ensuring timely diagnosis and treatment. The camp-based approach involves organizing camps in high-endemic areas twice a year, with detailed preparatory, implementation, and post-camp activities. The incentive-based approach focuses on training health workers to identify and refer suspected cases, with incentives provided for confirmed diagnoses. The country report or dossier for validating kala-azar elimination documents all evidence supporting the elimination of the disease. It includes historical and current data, health policies, surveillance systems, and program strategies. The report also outlines the epidemiology of kala-azar, the public health system's role, and the strategies for diagnosis, treatment, and vector control. Monitoring, quality control, and cross-border collaboration are essential components of the validation process. Definitions of control, elimination, and eradication are critical in public health. Control refers to reducing disease incidence, prevalence, morbidity, and mortality to acceptable levels through deliberate efforts, requiring ongoing interventions. Elimination of transmission means reducing infection incidence to zero in a defined area with minimal risk of reintroduction, requiring continued preventive actions. Elimination as a public health problem involves achieving measurable global targets set by the World Health Organization (WHO), with ongoing actions to maintain these targets. Eradication refers to the permanent reduction of a pathogen to zero, with no risk of reintroduction, while extinction means the pathogen no longer exists in nature or laboratories.
